newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Report to favour investment debate - WTO chief.
newsitem.headline: Report to favour investment debate - WTO chief.

text.p: World Trade Organisation chief Renato Ruggiero said on Tuesday a report by WTO analysts to be issued next week would make a "compelling case" for the controversial investment issue to be taken up in the body.

And in an address to a meeting of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), he urged developed and developing countries to recognise their economic interests lay with globalisation and not pursuit of national benefit.

"Foreign investment does not just supply the capital that developing countries so desperately need to supplement domestic savings; it has emerged as the central nervous system of the entire world economy," Ruggiero declared.

There was, he said, consensus among trading countries that trade and development were "intimately linked" in the context of globalisation and that the issues raised by the linkage needed further study and examination.

While investment issues had long been discussed in UNCTAD, a primary forum for trade and development problems, next week's report "makes a compelling case why trade and investment issues should be taken up also in the WTO," Ruggiero added.

The report is extracted from the first annual survey on world trade by the WTO -- which replaced the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) from January 1 1995 -- which is to be issued in November.

Ruggiero's speech came amid continuing debate among the WTO's 125 member countries, 90 of whom are emerging economies, on whether the problem should be on the agenda for the body's first ministerial conference in Singapore in December.

Many developing countries are opposed to bringing investment into the WTO, fearing the body's rules-based disciplines would force them to adopt investment policies that would limit their powers to nurture fledgling domestic industry.

At an informal meeting on Monday of ambassadors to the WTO to discuss the Singapore agenda, Canada and Japan presented a draft paper proposing that the ministers agree to set up a working party on investment.

The two have strong backing from the European Union, although the United States is reserving its position, preferring to focus on an investment agreement within the Paris-based Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).

There is strong resistance from some emerging economies, including India, Malaysia and Pakistan, although others -- in Asia and Latin America -- are ready for the discussion to be started at Singapore.

At Tuesday's meeting of UNCTAD's governing Trade and Development Board, Egypt and Cuba voiced clear reservations over bringing investment into the WTO. Egypt itself said it preferred to see discussion stay in the U.N. agency.

UNCTAD, which has just issued its own annual report on foreign direct investment (FDI) around the world, is hosting a forum on the problem later this week which has attracted international business leaders as well as ministers.

The UNCTAD report found that while FDI into developed and developing countries surged by 40 per cent in 1995 to $315 billion, but of this only $100 billion went to emerging economies and most of that went to a handful of states.
